opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think ImageNet supervised classification deserves a lot of credit. It's one of the main reasons the whole deep learning revolution in vision happened. You have about a million images and a thousand categories, a clean objective, and a clear benchmark. That combination lets people iterate on architectures very quickly: AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, and a lot of the work I did on things like ResNeXt all came out of that loop. The features also transferred surprisingly well. You could pretrain on ImageNet, fine-tune on detection or segmentation, and get big gains. So for almost a decade it was the default way to get a visual representation, and that wasn't an accident.

But the limitations become clear once you ask what the representation is actually learning. Classification compresses an entire image into one label out of a thousand. The objective tells the network to keep only the information that separates "golden retriever" from "Labrador," and it's free to throw away almost everything else: spatial layout, how objects relate to each other, counts, fine geometry, text in the scene. The network learns whatever shortcut is enough to get the label right, and sometimes that's texture rather than shape, or background rather than the object itself.

The second issue is the label space. A thousand fixed categories is a very narrow, human-defined view of the visual world, and it's skewed toward certain things, famously a lot of dog breeds. The real world is open-ended and long-tailed. You can't enumerate it with a fixed taxonomy, and human annotation doesn't scale to the amount of data you actually want.

That's a big part of why the field moved toward self-supervised learning, like contrastive methods and masked image modeling, and toward language supervision, like CLIP. With those you can use much more data without manual labels, and the supervision signal is richer. Masked autoencoding forces the model to reason about local structure, and language gives you an open vocabulary.

Even those approaches have their own blind spots, though. Something I've been thinking about a lot is that when we plug today's vision encoders into multimodal LLMs, the models still fail on very basic visual questions: orientation, counting, spatial relationships. Part of the reason is that CLIP-style training, like classification, is still mostly about matching an image to a global semantic description. So the deeper lesson from ImageNet, I think, is that the objective defines what "seeing" means for the model. If we want visual representations that support real understanding, maybe eventually world models, we need objectives that care about the structure of the visual world itself, not just which word goes with the picture.

So I'd summarize it this way. ImageNet classification was a brilliant bootstrap and an incredible engine for progress, but it gave us a fairly narrow notion of visual intelligence, and we're still working out what should replace it.

r001.rationale: The response credits ImageNet with strong transferable visual features and says its categories were skewed toward dog breeds.

r002.rationale: It says classification compresses an entire image into a single category label, capturing the constraint at the center of the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think ImageNet supervised classification is one of the most important things that happened to our field, and I say that as someone who has spent the last several years trying to move beyond it. So let me try to be fair to both sides.

The strength is really about scale and clarity. For the first time we had a million images with reasonably clean labels, a single objective, and a benchmark everyone agreed on. That did two things. It gave us a training signal strong enough that deep networks actually worked, and it gave us a shared ruler. When I was working on ResNeXt, or later ConvNeXt, the whole conversation was possible because we could say "same data, same recipe, here is the accuracy." Architecture research in particular benefited enormously. You could isolate a design choice, like grouped convolutions or the ordering of normalization and activation, and see its effect cleanly. And the features turned out to transfer surprisingly well. Pretrain on ImageNet, fine-tune on detection, segmentation, medical imaging, and you get a big boost. For a long time that was the default recipe for the entire industry.

The limitations become clearer the longer you live with it. The first is that classification is a very lossy objective. You are compressing an image into one of a thousand words. The network learns to throw away everything that does not help distinguish a golden retriever from a labrador. Spatial layout, geometry, relationships between objects, fine texture, all of that gets suppressed unless it happens to be discriminative for the label. So when you take those features to a dense task, you are often fighting the pretraining rather than building on it.

The second limitation is the label itself. ImageNet labels are human-chosen, object-centric, and single-label. Real images have many things in them, and the "correct" category is often arbitrary. We saw this with the relabeling work, where a lot of the remaining error was really label ambiguity. That ceiling tells you something: the objective has run out of signal before the model has run out of capacity.

The third is scaling. Supervised labels are expensive and they do not grow with the internet. So the moment you want to go from one million images to one billion, the supervised paradigm just stops. That pressure is what pushed many of us toward self-supervised methods, contrastive learning, masked image modeling, and then toward language-supervised models like CLIP, where the supervision is noisy but essentially free and far richer than a class index.

The last thing I would say is more about the culture than the method. ImageNet accuracy became such a strong attractor that for a while the field was optimizing the benchmark rather than the underlying question of what a good visual representation is. A lot of tricks that helped top-1 by a few tenths of a percent did not transfer anywhere. That is not the dataset's fault, but it is a cost.

So my overall assessment: ImageNet supervised learning was the right thing at the right time, it taught us how to train deep networks and gave us a common language, and its features are still a very strong baseline. But as a definition of "visual understanding" it is narrow, and the frontier has clearly moved toward objectives that preserve more of the image and scale with data rather than with annotation budgets. I think of it less as a paradigm we abandoned and more as the foundation that made the next one possible.

r002.rationale: It describes compressing an image into one of a thousand labels and notes that real images contain many things, while ImageNet uses single labels—capturing the constraint of assigning diverse visual content to one category.

astra-6.text:
I think ImageNet-style supervised learning has been incredibly useful. It gives us a clear objective and a consistent benchmark: can a model learn features that distinguish one category from another? And the interesting thing is that those features transfer. Even though you train for classification, the representation can be useful for detection, segmentation, and other tasks. So I wouldn’t dismiss classification as merely memorizing labels.

But the labels also define what the model is rewarded for preserving. If two images are both labeled “dog,” the objective doesn’t require the model to understand how their poses differ, where each dog is in the scene, or how it interacts with other objects. Some of that information may still be represented, but classification accuracy alone doesn’t tell you how much.

There’s also the possibility of taking shortcuts. A model can use background or texture cues that predict the label without learning the structure we hoped it would learn. Doing well on a benchmark is evidence of a useful capability, but it isn’t a complete measure of visual understanding.

So I see supervised classification as a very powerful starting point. The limitation is treating it as the entire problem. For more general visual representations, we need learning objectives and evaluations that capture more of what’s in an image than a single category label.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ImageNet-style supervised learning has been incredibly effective. You take a relatively simple task—predicting an image category—and, to do it well, the network learns features that transfer to many other tasks. That gave us a common benchmark and a very productive way to study architectures and optimization.

But the supervision also defines what the model is encouraged to preserve. If your goal is to recognize a dog, you want some invariance to its position, pose, or background. For classification, that’s useful. For other tasks, those details may be exactly what you need. A representation that’s good at assigning a category isn’t necessarily a representation that captures everything in the image.

There’s also the limitation of the label space. An image contains many objects, relationships, and attributes, and we compress that into one label. So I would separate two questions: how well can a model solve ImageNet, and how good is its visual representation more generally? They’re related, but they’re not the same question. Supervised classification is a powerful starting point; it shouldn’t be our complete definition of visual understanding.
